# F1: Authenticated User Profiles
<!-- packet-artifact-id:v1 {"uid":"4e5a34a1-db57-4e7b-9b1c-c406af3469d2","displayId":"F1","title":"Authenticated User Profiles"} -->
<!-- packet-change:v1 {"schemaVersion":1,"uid":"4e5a34a1-db57-4e7b-9b1c-c406af3469d2","displayId":"F1","status":"draft"} -->

**Status:** Draft

## Intent
Give signed-in users a persistent, identifiable account record so the product can recognize them across sessions and tailor experience.

## Current Behavior
None. No accounts, sign-up, sign-in, or persistent identity exist today.

## Desired Behavior
Users can create an account, authenticate to subsequent sessions, and maintain a profile (identity + attributes) stored persistently. Concrete fields and admin views to be finalized in interviews.

## Scope
- Account creation (sign-up) and deletion.
- Persistent storage of profile identity and attribute data.
- Session establishment and teardown upon successful/unsuccessful authentication.
- Retrieval of the currently authenticated user's own profile.

Out of scope (pending):
- Third-party OAuth identity providers (parked).
- Role/permission system beyond basic authenticated/unauthenticated (parked).
- Profile public sharing / lookup-by-email (parked).

## Affected Product Areas
- Identity / Accounts (new area)
- Storage (data persistence layer, newly introduced by this feature)

## Requirements
R1. Provide a mechanism for a new user to register and obtain a persisted account identifier.
R2. Allow an existing user to re-establish a trusted session using stored credentials.
R3. Expose a way for an authenticated user to retrieve their own profile data.
R4. Store profile data in the chosen storage backend; access restricted to the owning user except for fields marked publicly shareable.
R5. Support user-initiated account deactivation/deletion.
(Authentication mechanisms — password hashing algorithm, token format, session strategy — are deferred until the storage decision lands.)

## Decisions and Assumptions
D-F1.1. Authentication approach is intentionally decoupled from and gated behind the storage-backend decision. Rationale: scheme choice interacts strongly with storage characteristics (relational session table, embedded tokens, hash-at-rest columns).
A1. Greenfield; no pre-existing users, migrations, or compatibility burden assumed.

## Acceptance Criteria
AC1. After registration, a fresh browser/session can sign in with the same identity and retrieve the profile the user saved.
AC2. Unauthenticated requests cannot read or mutate any profile data.
AC3. Deleting/reactivating flow leaves a consistent audit trail per whatever standard quality gate we agree later.
(Additional ACs will be appended as auth scheme and fields are nailed down.)

options.label: Managed PostgreSQL (RDS/Neon/etc.)
options.reversibility: Medium — data migratable; ORM layer absorbs much variance.

options.summary: Relational rows for identities, hashed credentials, sessions; familiar query model.

benefits: Simple single-collection reads for a profile
consequences: Token/session typically kept in separate service/collection
costs: Weaker multi-document transactions historically (improved in v4+)

options.label: Hosted MongoDB Atlas
options.reversibility: Low-Medium — reshaping docs is easy early; painful once normalized.
risks: Growing complexity as we add relational-style relations (roles, relationships)
options.summary: Document-per-user with embedded sub-documents; flexible profile attrs.

benefits: Cheapest ops if profile grows binary assets
consequences: Split-brain auth/session logic possible if unmanaged carefully
costs: Two systems to reason about day one
options.label: Object store for blobs + lightweight KV for identity
options.reversibility: Low — splitting a coherent store apart later is messy.
risks: Over-engineered for a simple profile start
options.summary: Key-value for credentials/tokens; S3-class blob for richer profile payloads/files.

ramifications: Pick wrong → migration cost climbs steeply once users exist

recommendation.rationale: Greenfield with strong consistency needs (credentials, sessions); mature relational mapping keeps future role/audit work simpler.
